claim: Invasive bacterial disease is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in African children.
source: Invasive bacterial diseases are a major cause of child morbidity and mortality in Africa (Berkley et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Berkley et al., 2005

claim: Improved control measures, including the rollout of anti-bacterial conjugate vaccines, have led to recent declines in invasive bacterial disease burden.
source: Although improved control measures, including the rollout of anti-bacterial conjugate vaccines (Cowgill et al., 2006; Silaba et al., 2019), have led to recent declines, the burden of conditions such as pneumonia, meningitis, and sepsis secondary to bacterial pathogens remains significant (Vos, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cowgill et al., 2006; Silaba et al., 2019; and Vos, 2020

claim: The burden of conditions such as pneumonia, meningitis, and sepsis secondary to bacterial pathogens remains significant in Africa.
source: Although improved control measures, including the rollout of anti-bacterial conjugate vaccines (Cowgill et al., 2006; Silaba et al., 2019), have led to recent declines, the burden of conditions such as pneumonia, meningitis, and sepsis secondary to bacterial pathogens remains significant (Vos, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vos, 2020

claim: Susceptibility to invasive bacterial infections varies widely between individuals.
source: Susceptibility to invasive bacterial infections varies widely between individuals.
evidence: General statement based on established scientific knowledge

claim: In African children, some variability in susceptibility to invasive bacterial infections is determined by acquired comorbidities such as HIV, malnutrition, and malaria.
source: In African children, some of this variability is determined by acquired comorbidities such as HIV, malnutrition, and malaria (Berkley et al., 2005; Church and Maitland, 2014; Scott et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Berkley et al., 2005; Church and Maitland, 2014; Scott et al., 2011

claim: The identification of common genetic variants as determinants of bacterial infection suggests that a significant portion of variability in susceptibility is heritable.
source: However, the identification of common genetic variants as determinants of bacterial infection suggests that a significant portion of this variability is heritable.
evidence: Based on inference from genetic variant identification studies

claim: Many genetic susceptibility loci for bacterial infection have pathogen-specific effects.
source: Many of these genetic susceptibility loci have pathogen-specific effects (Davila et al., 2010; Gilchrist et al., 2018; Rautanen et al., 2016), which is consistent with our understanding of infection susceptibility derived from primary immunodeficiencies.
evidence: Supported by citations to Davila et al., 2010; Gilchrist et al., 2018; Rautanen et al., 2016

claim: Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease is an example of pathogen specificity among primary immunodeficiencies.
source: Key examples of pathogen specificity among primary immunodeficiencies include Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease and susceptibility to non-tuberculous mycobacteria and nontyphoidal Salmonella (Bustamante et al., 2014), terminal complement deficiencies and meningococcal disease (Figueroa et al., 1993), and IRAK4 deficiency and pneumococcal disease (Picard et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bustamante et al., 2014

claim: Terminal complement deficiencies are associated with meningococcal disease.
source: Key examples of pathogen specificity among primary immunodeficiencies include Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease and susceptibility to non-tuberculous mycobacteria and nontyphoidal Salmonella (Bustamante et al., 2014), terminal complement deficiencies and meningococcal disease (Figueroa et al., 1993), and IRAK4 deficiency and pneumococcal disease (Picard et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Figueroa et al., 1993

claim: IRAK4 deficiency is associated with pneumococcal disease.
source: Key examples of pathogen specificity among primary immunodeficiencies include Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease and susceptibility to non-tuberculous mycobacteria and nontyphoidal Salmonella (Bustamante et al., 2014), terminal complement deficiencies and meningococcal disease (Figueroa et al., 1993), and IRAK4 deficiency and pneumococcal disease (Picard et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Picard et al., 2007

claim: The rs334 A>T mutation in HBB (sickle haemoglobin) is associated with raised and lowered risks of infection secondary to a broad range of pathogens among homozygotes and heterozygotes, respectively.
source: A major exception to this is the rs334 A>T mutation in HBB (sickle haemoglobin), which is associated with raised and lowered risks of infection secondary to a broad range of pathogens among homozygotes (Williams et al., 2009) and heterozygotes (Scott et al., 2011), respectively.
evidence: Supported by citations to Williams et al., 2009 and Scott et al., 2011

claim: The effect sizes associated with sickle haemoglobin are extreme, being maintained in populations by balancing selection.
source: However, the effect sizes associated with sickle haemoglobin are extreme, being maintained in populations by balancing selection, and larger sample sizes will probably be needed for the discovery of new variants with multi-pathogen effects.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of sickle cell genetics and population genetics

claim: The clinical features of invasive bacterial infections and severe malaria are broadly similar.
source: Because the clinical features of invasive bacterial infections and severe malaria are broadly similar (Bejon et al., 2007), it can be difficult to distinguish between severe illness caused by extensive sequestration of malaria parasites in the microvasculature ('true' severe malaria) and bacterial sepsis in the presence of incidental parasitaemia on the basis of clinical features alone.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bejon et al., 2007

claim: It can be difficult to distinguish between 'true' severe malaria and bacterial sepsis in the presence of incidental parasitaemia on the basis of clinical features alone.
source: Because the clinical features of invasive bacterial infections and severe malaria are broadly similar (Bejon et al., 2007), it can be difficult to distinguish between severe illness caused by extensive sequestration of malaria parasites in the microvasculature ('true' severe malaria) and bacterial sepsis in the presence of incidental parasitaemia on the basis of clinical features alone.
evidence: Based on inference from clinical similarity and citation to Bejon et al., 2007

claim: Antibiotic pre-treatment and inadequate blood culture volumes mean that true invasive bacterial infections can often not be confirmed even in settings with excellent diagnostic facilities.
source: This is made harder still by the fact that antibiotic pre-treatment and inadequate blood culture volumes mean that, even in settings with excellent diagnostic facilities, true invasive bacterial infections can often not be confirmed (Driscoll et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Driscoll et al., 2017

claim: Approximately one-third of children recruited to studies in Africa with a clinical diagnosis of severe malaria were actually suffering from other conditions.
source: Recently, we illustrated this clinical complexity through a study in which we used probabilistic models based on malaria-specific biomarkers to show that approximately one-third of children recruited to studies in Africa with a clinical diagnosis of severe malaria were actually suffering from other conditions (Watson et al., 2021a; Watson et al., 2021b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Watson et al., 2021a and Watson et al., 2021b

claim: Invasive bacterial infections are common in children admitted to hospital with a clinical diagnosis of severe malaria, but in whom biomarkers subsequently suggest that malaria was probably not the primary cause for their severe illness.
source: In the current study, we extend this work to show that invasive bacterial infections are common in children admitted to hospital with a clinical diagnosis of severe malaria, but in whom biomarkers subsequently suggest that malaria was probably not the primary cause for their severe illness.
evidence: Based on data analysis presented in the study

claim: A dataset of genome-wide genotyped samples from 5400 Kenyan children was constructed, comprising critically unwell Kenyan children with bacteraemia and severe malaria, and population controls.
source: We then construct a dataset of genome-wide genotyped samples from 5400 Kenyan children, comprising critically unwell Kenyan children with bacteraemia (Rautanen et al., 2016) and severe malaria (Band, 2019), and population controls.
evidence: Based on data collection and methods described in the study

claim: A genome-wide association study (GWAS) of invasive bacterial infection in Kenyan children was performed, weighting cases according to the probability that their disease was mediated by a bacterial pathogen.
source: Using this dataset, we perform a genome-wide association study (GWAS) of invasive bacterial infection in Kenyan children, weighting cases according to the probability that their disease was mediated by a bacterial pathogen.
evidence: Based on methods and analysis described in the study

claim: BIRC6 was identified as a novel genetic determinant of invasive bacterial disease in Kenyan children.
source: In doing so, we increase our study power and identify BIRC6 as a novel genetic determinant of invasive bacterial disease in Kenyan children.
evidence: Based on GWAS results presented in the study

claim: Children admitted to the high dependency ward of Kilifi County Hospital with a clinical diagnosis of severe malaria between 11 June 1995 and 12 June 2008 were included in the study (n=2200).
source: Children admitted to the high dependency ward of Kilifi County Hospital with a clinical diagnosis of severe malaria, defined as a severe febrile illness in the presence of Plasmodium falciparum parasitaemia (n=2200), between 11 June 1995 and 12 June 2008 were included in the study.
evidence: Based on study recruitment data

claim: The definition of severe malaria used in the study is sensitive but not specific, meaning that the study included some children with sepsis accompanied by incidental parasitaemia.
source: While this definition is sensitive it is not specific, meaning that our study will have included some children with sepsis accompanied by incidental parasitaemia (Watson et al., 2021a).
evidence: Based on inference from the definition used and citation to Watson et al., 2021a

claim: Two probabilistic models were used to determine the likelihood of 'true' severe malaria among children with a clinical diagnosis of severe malaria.
source: We therefore used two probabilistic models, which included either platelet counts and plasma PfHRP2 concentrations (Model 1, n=1400) or white blood cell and platelet counts (Model 2, n=2200), to determine the likelihood of 'true' severe malaria among these children.
evidence: Based on methods described in the study

claim: Of 1400 children with a clinical diagnosis of severe malaria with measured plasma PfHRP2 concentrations, 425 (30.4%) had a low probability (P(SM|Data)<0.5) of having 'true' severe malaria.
source: Of 1400 children with a clinical diagnosis of severe malaria with measured plasma PfHRP2 concentrations, 425 (30.4%, Figure 1A and B) had a low probability (P(SM|Data)<0.5) of having 'true' severe malaria (941 of 2220 children using WBC and platelet count data, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Based on data analysis and shown in Figure 1A and B

claim: White blood counts in isolation were not associated with risk of concurrent bacteraemia.
source: Conversely, white blood counts in isolation were not associated with risk of concurrent bacteraemia (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The GWAS of bacteraemia failed to identify genetic correlates of bacteraemia risk beyond the sickle cell locus.
source: Despite this, our GWAS of bacteraemia failed to identify genetic correlates of bacteraemia risk beyond the sickle cell locus (Rautanen et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on GWAS results and citation to Rautanen et al., 2016

claim: Following quality control measures, 1445 cases of culture-confirmed bacteraemia, 1143 cases of severe malaria, and 2812 control children were included in the analysis.
source: Following quality control measures (see Materials and methods), we included 1445 cases of culture-confirmed bacteraemia, 1143 cases of severe malaria, and 2812 control children in our current analysis (Table 2, Figure 2).
evidence: Based on data after quality control, shown in Table 2 and Figure 2

claim: Fine mapping of the association identified a credible set of seven SNPs with a 95% probability of containing the causal variant, spanning a 212 kb region: chr2:32,402,640–32,614,746.
source: Fine mapping of this association identified a credible set of seven SNPs with a 95% probability of containing the causal variant (Table 3), spanning a 212 kb region: chr2:32,402,640–32,614,746.
evidence: Based on fine mapping analysis shown in Table 3

claim: Genotype was not associated with invasive bacterial disease risk in the Kauma subpopulation.
source: Genotype was not associated with invasive bacterial disease risk in the Kauma subpopulation, however the sample size in the stratum is very limited (154 cases, 318 controls) and may simply reflect insufficient power to detect an association.
evidence: Based on stratified analysis with limited sample size

claim: An independent case-control collection of Kenyan children with bacteraemia (n=434) and healthy controls (n=1258) was used for replication.
source: We sought to replicate evidence of association in our discovery analysis through use of an independent case-control collection of Kenyan children with bacteraemia (n=434) and healthy controls (n=1258) conducted in the same population.
evidence: Based on replication study design

claim: The association was driven by children with culture-confirmed bacteraemia and critically unwell children with malaria parasites, but a low probability of 'true' severe malaria.
source: That association was driven by children with culture-confirmed bacteraemia and critically unwell children with malaria parasites, but a low probability of 'true' severe malaria.
evidence: Based on stratified analysis

claim: The data best-supported a model in which genotype increases risk of bacteraemia caused by a broad range of pathogens, including bacteraemia secondary to pneumococcus, nontyphoidal Salmonellae, Escherichia coli, β-haemolytic streptococci, Staphylococcus aureus, and other less common pathogens grouped as a single stratum (log10 Bayes factor = 4.72).
source: In that analysis, the data best-supported a model in which genotype increases risk of bacteraemia caused by a broad range of pathogens, including bacteraemia secondary to pneumococcus, nontyphoidal Salmonellae, Escherichia coli, β-haemolytic streptococci, Staphylococcus aureus, and other less common pathogens grouped as a single stratum (log10 Bayes factor = 4.72).
evidence: Based on Bayesian model comparison analysis

claim: Genotype at rs183868412 similarly modified risk of bacteraemia in the neonatal period and in older children (log10 Bayes factor = 2.70).
source: Genotype at rs183868412 similarly modified risk of bacteraemia in the neonatal period and in older children (log10 Bayes factor = 2.70, Figure 5B).
evidence: Based on Bayesian model comparison analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: Malaria infection results in increased risk of invasive bacterial disease secondary to a broad range of pathogens.
source: Malaria infection results in increased risk of invasive bacterial disease secondary to a broad range of pathogens (Scott et al., 2011), and genetic determinants of malaria risk (e.g. sickle cell trait) modify risk of bacterial infection in malaria-endemic settings (Scott et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Scott et al., 2011

claim: Genetic determinants of malaria risk (e.g. sickle cell trait) modify risk of bacterial infection in malaria-endemic settings.
source: Malaria infection results in increased risk of invasive bacterial disease secondary to a broad range of pathogens (Scott et al., 2011), and genetic determinants of malaria risk (e.g. sickle cell trait) modify risk of bacterial infection in malaria-endemic settings (Scott et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Scott et al., 2011

claim: The effect of genetic variation at BIRC6 on invasive bacterial disease risk operates independently of malaria.
source: The observation that, among children with a clinical diagnosis of severe malaria, risk of disease is only modified by rs183868412 in children with a low probability that their disease represents 'true' severe malaria (Figure 5) suggests that the effect of genetic variation at BIRC6 on invasive bacterial disease risk operates independently of malaria.
evidence: Based on inference from stratified analysis shown in Figure 5

claim: The data best-supports an effect of rs183868412 genotype on bacteraemia risk in children both with and without concomitant parasitaemia (log10 Bayes factor = 2.73).
source: In keeping with this, the data best-supports an effect of rs183868412 genotype on bacteraemia risk in children both with and without concomitant parasitaemia (log10 Bayes factor = 2.73, Figure 5C).
evidence: Based on Bayesian model comparison analysis shown in Figure 5C

claim: Unlike sickle cell trait, the increased risk of invasive bacterial infection conferred by rs183868412:T carriage in the study setting is stable across a period of declining malaria prevalence (Bayes factor = 8.7).
source: In addition, unlike sickle cell trait (Scott et al., 2011), the increased risk of invasive bacterial infection conferred by rs183868412:T carriage in the study setting is stable across a period of declining malaria prevalence (Bayes factor = 8.7, Figure 5D).
evidence: Based on Bayesian model comparison analysis shown in Figure 5D and citation to Scott et al., 2011

claim: The derived allele rs183868412:T, associated with increased risk of invasive bacterial disease in Kenyan children, is absent in non-African populations.
source: The derived allele rs183868412:T, associated with increased risk of invasive bacterial disease in Kenyan children, is absent in non-African populations (https://gnomad.broadinstitute.org).
evidence: Based on data from gnomAD database

claim: Within Africa, rs183868412:T is present in all nine African populations included in the MalariaGEN consortium project, with MAFs ranging from 0.011 in The Gambia to 0.034 in Malawi.
source: Within Africa, rs183868412:T is present in all nine African populations included in the MalariaGEN consortium project (Band, 2019; Table 6), MAFs ranging from 0.011 in The Gambia to 0.034 in Malawi.
evidence: Based on data from MalariaGEN consortium shown in Table 6 and citation to Band, 2019

claim: rs183868412 is associated with alternative splicing of BIRC6 in stimulated monocytes.
source: rs183868412 is associated with alternative splicing of BIRC6 in stimulated monocytes
evidence: Based on eQTL analysis described in the section

claim: There was no evidence for a regulatory effect of rs183868412 at the gene level in monocytes regardless of stimulation.
source: We found no evidence for a regulatory effect of rs183868412 at the gene level in monocytes regardless of stimulation.
evidence: Based on eQTL mapping analysis

claim: The effect of rs183868412 on BIRC6 exon expression was only observed following stimulation with Pam3CSK4.
source: This effect was only observed following stimulation with Pam3CSK4 (Figure 6), with the bacteraemia risk allele, rs183868412:T, being associated with reduced expression of this sequence.
evidence: Based on eQTL mapping analysis shown in Figure 6

claim: The bacteraemia risk allele, rs183868412:T, is associated with reduced expression of the 12 bp BIRC6 exonic sequence.
source: This effect was only observed following stimulation with Pam3CSK4 (Figure 6), with the bacteraemia risk allele, rs183868412:T, being associated with reduced expression of this sequence.
evidence: Based on eQTL mapping analysis shown in Figure 6

claim: Increased risk of invasive bacterial disease may be associated with decreased expression of an alternative BIRC6 transcript in TLR1/2-stimulated monocytes.
source: Thus, increased risk of invasive bacterial disease may be associated with decreased expression of an alternative BIRC6 transcript in TLR1/2-stimulated monocytes.
evidence: Based on inference from eQTL and splicing analysis

claim: BIRC6 (Baculovirus inhibitor of apoptosis protein repeat containing 6), also known as BRUCE (BIR repeat containing ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme), encodes a large member of the inhibitor of apoptosis protein (IAP) family.
source: BIRC6 (Baculovirus inhibitor of apoptosis protein repeat containing 6), also known as BRUCE (BIR repeat containing ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme), encodes a large member of the inhibitor of apoptosis protein (IAP) family (Hauser et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hauser et al., 1998

claim: Members of the IAP family bind to cognate caspases, inhibiting their activity through occlusion of their active site.
source: Members of the IAP family bind to cognate caspases, inhibiting their activity, and thereby cell death, through occlusion of their active site (Verhagen et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Verhagen et al., 2001

claim: A proportion of IAPs also contain an E3 ubiquitin ligase allowing both direct inhibition of caspases and targeting of caspases for proteasomal degradation.
source: A proportion of IAPs also contain an E3 ubiquitin ligase allowing both direct inhibition of caspases and targeting of caspases for proteasomal degradation (Verhagen et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Verhagen et al., 2001

claim: BIRC6 contains both inhibitor of apoptosis domains and an E2/E3 ubiquitin ligase, which function to inhibit apoptosis in response to a variety of stimuli.
source: BIRC6 contains both inhibitor of apoptosis domains and an E2/E3 ubiquitin ligase, which function to inhibit apoptosis in response to a variety of stimuli, both by interaction with and degradation of caspase-9, but also through the ubiquitination and degradation of SMAC, an IAP antagonist (Hao et al., 2004; Bartke et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hao et al., 2004 and Bartke et al., 2004

claim: BIRC6 regulates autophagosome-lysosome fusion.
source: BIRC6 also regulates autophagosome-lysosome fusion (Ebner et al., 2018), and ubiquitinates (and targets for degradation) LC3, a key effector of autophagosome formation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ebner et al., 2018

claim: BIRC6 ubiquitinates (and targets for degradation) LC3, a key effector of autophagosome formation.
source: BIRC6 also regulates autophagosome-lysosome fusion (Ebner et al., 2018), and ubiquitinates (and targets for degradation) LC3, a key effector of autophagosome formation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of BIRC6 function

claim: BIRC6 acts as a negative regulator of autophagy.
source: Thus, BIRC6 also acts as a negative regulator of autophagy (Jia and Bonifacino, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jia and Bonifacino, 2019

claim: Sepsis induces marked changes in apoptosis across a range of immune cells.
source: Sepsis induces marked changes in apoptosis across a range of immune cells (Hotchkiss and Nicholson, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hotchkiss and Nicholson, 2006

claim: There is markedly enhanced apoptosis in both dendritic cells and in lymphocytes during sepsis.
source: There is markedly enhanced apoptosis in both dendritic cells (Hotchkiss et al., 2002) and in lymphocytes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hotchkiss et al., 2002

claim: Enhanced lymphocyte apoptosis is most striking in B cells and CD4+ T cells.
source: Enhanced lymphocyte apoptosis is most striking in B cells and CD4+ T cells (Hotchkiss et al., 2001) which, at least in part, is mediated by caspase-9.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hotchkiss et al., 2001

claim: The consequent lymphopoenia from sepsis-induced apoptosis is correlated with both severity of sepsis and outcome.
source: The consequent lymphopoenia is correlated with both severity of sepsis and outcome (Le Tulzo et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Le Tulzo et al., 2002

claim: Sepsis-induced apoptosis induces immune cell dysfunction, phagocytosis of apoptotic cells resulting in reduction in pro-inflammatory cytokine production, and cross-presentation of antigen from apoptotic cells to adaptive immune cells.
source: In addition to the direct effects of immune cell loss on the innate and adaptive immune responses to invasive infection, sepsis-induced apoptosis induces immune cell dysfunction, phagocytosis of apoptotic cells resulting in reduction in pro-inflammatory cytokine production, and cross-presentation of antigen from apoptotic cells to adaptive immune cells (Albert, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Albert, 2004

claim: Members of the IAP family, including NAIP/BIRC1 and BIRC3, are downregulated in immune cells in patients with sepsis.
source: In keeping with a role for regulators of apoptosis in the pathogenesis of sepsis, members of the IAP family, including NAIP/BIRC1 and BIRC3, are downregulated in immune cells in patients with sepsis, as is the BIRC6 ubiquitination target SMAC (Hoogerwerf et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hoogerwerf et al., 2010

claim: The BIRC6 ubiquitination target SMAC is downregulated in immune cells in patients with sepsis.
source: In keeping with a role for regulators of apoptosis in the pathogenesis of sepsis, members of the IAP family, including NAIP/BIRC1 and BIRC3, are downregulated in immune cells in patients with sepsis, as is the BIRC6 ubiquitination target SMAC (Hoogerwerf et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hoogerwerf et al., 2010

claim: Autophagy contributes to the direct removal of intracellular pathogens and, through the degradation of invading organisms in autophagosomes, directs antigen presentation and pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion.
source: Autophagy contributes to the direct removal of intracellular pathogens and, through the degradation of invading organisms in autophagosomes, directs antigen presentation and pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion (Deretic et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Deretic et al., 2013

claim: BIRC6 regulates autophagy through its interaction with LC3.
source: As above, BIRC6 regulates autophagy through its interaction with LC3, and overexpression of LC3B limits inflammation and tissue injury in a mouse model of sepsis (Lo et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on established knowledge and citation to Lo et al., 2013

claim: Overexpression of LC3B limits inflammation and tissue injury in a mouse model of sepsis.
source: As above, BIRC6 regulates autophagy through its interaction with LC3, and overexpression of LC3B limits inflammation and tissue injury in a mouse model of sepsis (Lo et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lo et al., 2013

claim: Genetic variation at BIRC6 plays a role in determining risk of invasive infection secondary to a broad range of bacteria.
source: In keeping with a role for BIRC6 in autophagy and apoptosis in sepsis, our data identify a role for genetic variation at BIRC6 in determining risk of invasive infection secondary to a broad range of bacteria.
evidence: Based on GWAS and functional data presented in the study

claim: Previously published data describing susceptibility to invasive bacterial infection has highlighted a prominent role for genetic risk factors that are specific to single pathogens.
source: This is in contrast to previously published data describing susceptibility to invasive bacterial infection, which has highlighted a prominent role for genetic risk factors that are specific to single pathogens (Davila et al., 2010; Gilchrist et al., 2018; Rautanen et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Davila et al., 2010; Gilchrist et al., 2018; Rautanen et al., 2016

claim: The derived allele (T) at rs183868412 was associated with increased risk of bacteraemia secondary to gram-positive (β-haemolytic streptococci, S. pneumoniae, and S. aureus) and gram-negative (E. coli, nontyphoidal Salmonella) pathogens, including intracellular and extracellular bacteria, and enteric and respiratory pathogens.
source: In this study, the derived allele (T) at rs183868412 was associated with increased risk of bacteraemia secondary to gram-positive (β-haemolytic streptococci, S. pneumoniae, and S. aureus) and gram-negative (E. coli, nontyphoidal Salmonella) pathogens, including intracellular and extracellular bacteria, and enteric and respiratory pathogens.
evidence: Based on pathogen-stratified analysis presented in the study

claim: rs183868412 modified risk of bacteraemia in both the neonatal period, when infection is likely to be maternally derived, and in older children, when sources of community acquired infection will be more diverse.
source: Moreover, rs183868412 modified risk of bacteraemia in both the neonatal period, when infection is likely to be maternally derived, and in older children, when sources of community acquired infection will be more diverse.
evidence: Based on age-stratified analysis presented in the study

claim: The modulation of invasive bacterial disease risk by genetic variation at BIRC6, despite diverse sources and routes of infection and diverse mechanisms of invasion, suggests a mechanism in which genetic variation at BIRC6 modifies risk of invasive infection downstream of initial mechanisms of infection and invasion.
source: This modulation of invasive bacterial disease risk, despite diverse sources and routes of infection and diverse mechanisms of invasion, suggests a mechanism in which genetic variation at BIRC6 modifies risk of invasive infection downstream of initial mechanisms of infection and invasion.
evidence: Based on inference from the broad pathogen effects observed

claim: Common genetic variation at another ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme, UBE2U, has been shown to modify outcome in meningitis secondary to diverse pathogens in individuals of European ancestry.
source: In an interesting parallel to this, common genetic variation at another ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme, UBE2U, has been shown to modify outcome in meningitis secondary to diverse pathogens in individuals of European ancestry (Lees et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lees et al., 2019

claim: The African-specific nature of the trait-associated variation identified limits the ability to comprehensively interrogate the effect of that variation in immune cells.
source: The African-specific nature of the trait-associated variation identified here limits our ability to comprehensively interrogate the effect of that variation in immune cells.
evidence: Based on discussion of study limitations

claim: The eQTL mapping data utilized is limited in that it allows consideration of only a single immune cell type.
source: The eQTL mapping data that we utilise here (Quach et al., 2016) is limited in that it allows us only to consider a single immune cell type.
evidence: Based on discussion of study limitations and citation to Quach et al., 2016

claim: The splicing signal at BIRC6 is based on only 10 individuals heterozygous for rs183868412:T.
source: It is also important to note that there are relatively few African-ancestry individuals in the eQTL mapping data we utilise here, and the splicing signal at BIRC6 is based on only 10 individuals heterozygous for rs183868412:T.
evidence: Based on discussion of study limitations

claim: There is a paucity of large-scale genetic association studies performed in African populations.
source: In addition, there is a paucity of large-scale genetic association studies performed in African populations.
evidence: Based on general knowledge of the field

claim: The African-specific nature of the variation identified limits the ability to explore pleiotropic effects at this locus.
source: The African-specific nature of the variation identified in our study therefore limits our ability to explore pleiotropic effects at this locus.
evidence: Based on discussion of study limitations

claim: The low MAF of rs183868412 will result in very limited power to detect selection events at the locus.
source: Allied to this, the low MAF of rs183868412 will result in very limited power to detect selection events at the locus.
evidence: Based on inference from population genetics principles

claim: The study uses plasma PfHRP2 concentrations to help identify children at low risk of 'true' severe malaria.
source: Our study uses plasma PfHRP2 concentrations to help identify children at low risk of 'true' severe malaria.
evidence: Based on methods described in the study

claim: There is increasing frequency of pfhrp2 and pfhrp3 deletions in many settings, including in Africa.
source: Given the increasing frequency of pfhrp2 and pfhrp3 deletions in many settings, including in Africa (Agaba et al., 2019; Feleke et al., 2021; Gamboa et al., 2010), an understanding of the local prevalence of pfhrp2/3 deletions will be important in considering how to translate this model to other settings.
evidence: Supported by citations to Agaba et al., 2019; Feleke et al., 2021; Gamboa et al., 2010

claim: The data identify a role for BIRC6 in the pathogenesis of invasive bacterial infections in Kenyan children.
source: Taken together, our data identify a role for BIRC6 in the pathogenesis of invasive bacterial infections in Kenyan children.
evidence: Based on the overall findings of the study

claim: By maximising available sample size to include children with a high likelihood of invasive bacterial infection, but without culture-confirmed infection, novel variant discovery is facilitated and a common genetic architecture of invasive bacterial disease secondary to diverse pathogens is revealed.
source: By maximising our available sample size to include children with a high likelihood of invasive bacterial infection, but without culture-confirmed infection, we facilitate novel variant discovery and reveal a common genetic architecture of invasive bacterial disease secondary to diverse pathogens.
evidence: Based on the study design and findings

claim: The data expand understanding of the biology of invasive infection in African children.
source: In doing so, we expand our understanding of the biology of invasive infection in African children.
evidence: Based on the overall contribution of the study

claim: The data inform understanding of the biology shared by diverse bacterial infections causing a common clinical syndrome: sepsis.
source: In particular, these data inform our understanding of the biology shared by diverse bacterial infections causing a common clinical syndrome: sepsis.
evidence: Based on the overall contribution of the study
